chunks: "Setup time is how long the data input has to be stable before the active clock edge so the flip-flop can capture it reliably.
Hold time is how long it has to stay stable after the edge. Together they define a small window around the edge where the data must not change.
The reason is that inside the flip-flop the input has to propagate through internal gates and settle onto a latch before the clock closes it.
If data arrives too late, that is a setup violation; if it changes too soon after the edge, the master latch hasn't finished closing and that's a hold violation.

If you violate either, the flip-flop can capture the wrong value, or worse, go metastable, where Q hovers at an in-between voltage for a while and may resolve randomly, and downstream logic can see inconsistent values.
For a path between two flip-flops, setup says the clock period has to be at least clock-to-Q plus the logic delay plus setup time plus skew.
You fix a setup violation by slowing the clock or shortening the logic.

Hold says clock-to-Q plus the shortest logic delay has to exceed the hold time plus skew, and that doesn't depend on frequency, so you can't fix it by slowing the clock; you add delay on the data path."
